title: Colossians 3:1–11
context: After Colossians 2’s warning against hollow philosophy, Paul grounds holy living in union with the risen Christ—seek the things above, put to death earthly vices, and put on the new man where ethnic and social barriers fall before Christ who is all and in all.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Colossians 3:1–11.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: If ye are risen, seek the things above - As Christ being risen, immediately went to heaven. For ye are dead - To the things on earth. And your real, spiritual life is hid from the world, and laid up in God, with Christ - Who hath merited, promised, prepared it for us, and gives us the earnest and foretaste of it in our hearts.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Col 3:1–11)

reformed.quote: Ascension follows resurrection: hence, if we are the members of Christ we must ascend into heaven, because he, on being raised up from the dead, was received up into heaven, (Mark 16:19,) that he might draw us up with him. Now, we seek those things which are above, when in our minds we are truly sojourners in this world, and are not bound to it.

verses.text: If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The “if” assumes a sharing in Christ’s resurrection for those who are His. Because they have been raised with Him, they are summoned to seek what is above—where the seated Christ reigns.

Prevenient and renewing grace make this seeking possible; the command still calls for responsible pursuit. Heavenly-mindedness is not escape from earth but obedience oriented to the risen Lord.
verses.reformedNotes:
Union language frames the ethic: those raised with Christ already share His resurrection life. The imperative rests on indicative grace already given in Him.

Seek what is above because Christ is seated at God’s right hand. Sanctification flows from that union; the throne of the exalted Lord defines the believer’s true north.
verses.keyContrast: Both ground seeking in resurrection union with Christ. Arminians press grace that enables a resistible-in-principle pursuit of heavenly things; Calvinists emphasize effectual union that already relocates the believer’s life and makes seeking the fruit of that bond.

verses.text: Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mind-setting is deliberate. Paul contrasts above with earth—not as hatred of creation but as refusal to let earthly measures rule the heart.

Arminian interpreters hear a grace-enabled charge: the Spirit illumines and strengthens, yet believers must not drift back to earthbound fixation. Attention is a moral act under assisting grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
The renewed mind is redirected to Christ’s realm. Earthly things are not denied as God’s gifts, but they must not claim lordship over affection and thought.

Providence and union teach where to look. The Spirit who raised Christ also reorders meditation so that earthly cares sit under heavenly priority.

verses.text: For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Death with Christ explains the new orientation: the old life’s claim is broken. Life “hidden with Christ in God” is secure yet not fully unveiled—identity is located in Him, not in visible status.

Grace places life in Christ’s keeping; believers remain responsible to live from that hidden identity and not dig up what died with Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Participatory death and hidden life are gospel facts, not mere metaphors. The believer’s true life is concealed in Christ within God—safe beyond the world’s verdict.

What God has hidden in the Son cannot finally be lost to earthly failure. Identity is Christ-held; sanctification works out what union has already secured.
verses.keyContrast: Both confess death-with-Christ and a life hidden in Him. Arminians emphasize a grace-wrought status that calls for ongoing, non-coerced faithfulness; Reformed interpreters emphasize an effectual, God-kept union that grounds assurance while still commanding holy living.

verses.text: When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory.
verses.arminianNotes:
Christ is “your life”—present possession—and His appearing will unveil shared glory. Hope looks forward without denying present responsibility.

The sincere promise of appearing with Him strengthens perseverance. Those who remain in Him by grace-enabled faith will share His glory when He is revealed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ Himself is the believer’s life; future appearing with Him in glory is certain for those united to Him. Eschatology crowns present union.

Glory is not self-earned unveiling but the public display of what God has already hidden in His Son. Hope rests on Christ’s appearing, not on fragile self-assessment.

verses.text: Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore” ties mortification to resurrection life. Paul names desires that enthrone the self and calls covetousness idolatry—wrong love of goods is false worship.

Enabling grace makes killing sin possible; the command is no formality. Believers must not toy with earthly lusts they once walked in, but actively put them to death.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mortification is the necessary fruit of having died and been raised with Christ. The catalogue exposes heart-idols, climaxing in covetousness as worship of created things.

The Spirit works death to sin in those united to Christ. The imperative assumes regenerating power already given; holy severity toward lust is gratitude, not self-salvation.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat putting sin to death as non-negotiable. Arminians underline grace-enabled, responsible mortification that must not be resisted; Reformed interpreters stress Spirit-effectual killing of sin as the outworking of union with the crucified and risen Christ.

verses.text: For these things’ sake the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wrath is coming—not theatrical scare but moral seriousness. Earthly vices invite God’s settled opposition to evil.

The same God who sincerely offers mercy also judges unrepented idolatry. Grace that enables repentance makes the warning a call to turn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Divine wrath against these practices is certain and just. Paul’s is coming keeps eschatological judgment before the church’s eyes.

Holiness is not optional polish. Those delivered from wrath in Christ still hear why the old walk was lethal—and why providence will not finally wink at idolatry.

verses.text: You also once walked in those, when you lived in them,
verses.arminianNotes:
Paul reminds them of a former walk—living in the vices they must now kill. Memory of grace-rescued past fuels gratitude, not nostalgia.

Pastorally: they once lived there; they need not return. Enabling grace has opened a new path; remaining in the old life would be culpable refusal of light already given.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Once” marks a decisive break wrought by God’s saving work. They lived in those things; they do so no longer as their defining realm.

Recalling the old walk magnifies mercy. Conversion is God’s transfer of dominion; the past is confessed so that present holiness looks like belonging to Christ.

verses.text: but now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But now” shifts from sexual and covetous sins to relational toxins of speech and temper. Putting away is comprehensive—“all.”

Grace that cleansed the walk also summons clean mouths and hearts. Believers remain responsible to cast off anger’s chain before it hardens into malice and slander.
verses.reformedNotes:
The new era (“now”) demands disposal of old community poisons. Speech sins destroy the body Christ is forming.

Putting away is Spirit-wrought fruit of the new creation. The church’s speech should match those raised with Christ, not the old humanity’s rage and contempt.

verses.text: Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings,
verses.arminianNotes:
Lying is banned among those who have already put off the old man. The indicative—“you have put off”—grounds the imperative against falsehood.

Conversion includes a break with the old self’s practices; grace enabled that putting off, and ongoing honesty is the fitting response we must not refuse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Truth-telling belongs to those who have shed the old self. The aorist “put off” points to a decisive gospel change already accomplished in union with Christ.

Ethics follow identity. Because the old man is discarded with his practices, lying contradicts who they already are in Christ.
verses.keyContrast: Both tie honesty to having put off the old man. Arminians typically press a grace-enabled change that still requires continual, non-coerced obedience; Reformed interpreters usually press a decisive, God-wrought stripping of the old man whose practices no longer define the elect.

verses.text: and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator,
verses.arminianNotes:
Putting on the new self pairs with putting off the old. Renewal is ongoing—“being renewed”—in knowledge patterned after the Creator’s image.

Grace restores the image through growing knowledge of God; believers cooperate with that renewing work and must not resist the Spirit’s shaping.
verses.reformedNotes:
The new self is donned in Christ and continually renewed by God toward the Creator’s image. Knowledge here is transformative, not mere data.

Sanctification is God’s progressive remaking of those united to Christ. The image spoiled in Adam is restored by the Creator’s own renewing power.
verses.keyContrast: Both celebrate the new self renewed toward God’s image. Arminians stress ongoing, grace-enabled cooperation in that renewal; Reformed readers emphasize God’s effectual renewing work in those already clothed with the new self in Christ.

verses.text: where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, or free person; but Christ is all, and in all.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the new-self community, ethnic, ritual, cultural, and status barriers lose their dividing power. Christ is all—and in all who belong to Him.

The gospel’s sincere breadth gathers every kind of person into one renewed people. No pedigree or chains define worth where Christ fills the field of vision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Union with Christ dissolves the old humanity’s ranking systems. Greek/Jew, rite, culture, and bondage/freedom are not ultimate; Christ is all and in all His people.

The church’s unity is Christ-centered, not sentiment. Those He indwells share one new identity that relativizes every earthly hierarchy without denying creaturely callings.
